before.supportingExcerpt: HER2 is an orphan receptor without a known direct activating ligand. Its partner HER3 binds neuregulin. Diwanji and colleagues studied the HER2-HER3-NRG1-beta complex, including defined mutant and purified-complex experiments, so a generic growth factor drawn directly on HER2 would assign the wrong binding partner. Antibody binding, disruption of an assembled complex and inhibition of activation are separate outcomes; the mutant-complex results do not define every antibody response in an unmodified tumour.

points.requirement: A generic epithelial lining has an extracellular basement membrane distinct from each cell plasma membrane; the drawing is not a universal breast blueprint or invasion test.

The relevant compartments depend on the tissue and disease.

points.requirement: A hypothetical single chain has two folded domains connected by one linker; an intrachain interface is the meeting of apposed surfaces, not an empty cleft, extra material or demonstrated covalent fusion.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Primary structure describes sequence; secondary structure describes local arrangements; tertiary structure describes a chain’s organization; quaternary structure describes assembly between chains. These are levels of description, rather than four obligatory stages. A domain is a recognizable structural unit; a motif is a recurring sequence or structural pattern. An interface is a contact surface and can combine residues far apart in sequence. Intrinsically disordered regions can have normal functions without one stable isolated fold.
evidence.explanation: An interface is an apposed contact surface, while the two-domain example supplies one chain and one linker. points.requirement: A selected serine-site kinase reaction transfers phosphate from ATP to the same protein oxygen, producing ADP and modified site. P denotes a phosphate group; molecule drawings are not protein abundance measurements.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Protein kinases commonly transfer phosphate from ATP to a substrate, producing ADP. Protein phosphatases remove phosphate by hydrolysis without regenerating ATP. A modification can affect catalysis, binding, localization or interactions; sites on one protein can have different functions. Src experiments demonstrated an inhibitory tail-phosphorylation mechanism in their defined preparation, so phosphorylation should not be treated as universal activation.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional comparison, sample A has a phosphopeptide signal of 1 and a parent-protein signal of 1; sample B has signals of 2 and 2 on the same relative scale. evidence.supportingExcerpt: A full agonist can reach a system’s maximal measured response. Competing partial agonists can reduce a full agonist’s response when they replace it. A neutral antagonist opposes agonist action without changing agonist-independent baseline activity; an inverse agonist reduces that activity when it is measurable. Antagonism need not use the agonist’s binding site.

points.requirement: A possible branched relay distinguishes kinase phosphate transfer from RAS GTP/GDP switching and scaffolds holding partners; not every relay is a kinase or every phosphate activating.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Many protein kinases transfer phosphate from ATP to selected substrate residues, commonly serine, threonine or tyrosine, leaving ADP. Phosphatases remove phosphate through a different reaction, rather than simply making ATP by reversing kinase activity. Kinases can also modify lipids, as PI3K does. Protein amount is distinct from catalytic activity, and not every relay protein is a kinase. In the defined EGFR asymmetric-dimer mechanism, activation-loop phosphorylation was not required for activation.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional comparison, sample A has a phosphopeptide signal of 1 and a parent-protein signal of 1; sample B has signals of 2 and 2 on the same relative scale.
